case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a criminal defendant’s broad plea-agreement appeal waiver bars appellate review of a due-process challenge to a supervised-release condition when the sentencing judge later states the defendant “has a right to appeal” and the government does not object.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Enforcement of plea-agreement appeal waivers (contract-based doctrine under federal common law and Rule 11 plea colloquy principles), applied to an appeal from a federal conviction and sentence under 18 U.S.C. § 3742 and related appellate jurisdiction statutes; the underlying claim invokes the Due Process Clause (Fifth Amendment) as applied to supervised-release conditions.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that the Fifth Circuit enforces appeal waivers too rigidly by recognizing only narrow exceptions (typically ineffective assistance of counsel or a sentence above the statutory maximum), and that his appeal should be heard because (a) due-process challenges to supervised-release conditions should not be categorically foreclosed by a general waiver, and/or (b) the waiver became unenforceable (or was effectively superseded/waived) when the district court advised at sentencing that he had a right to appeal and the government did not object, creating reasonable reliance and undermining the knowing-and-voluntary nature or enforceability of the waiver in these circumstances.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that petitioner knowingly and voluntarily agreed to waive any appeal on any ground other than ineffective assistance of counsel, that the waiver’s text covers his challenge to the supervised-release condition (including a due-process theory), and that a generic, unobjected-to statement by the sentencing judge at the end of sentencing that the defendant “has a right to appeal” does not nullify or modify a valid plea waiver; therefore the Fifth Circuit correctly dismissed the appeal based on the waiver.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s forfeiture theory usefully highlights that the Government can waive reliance on an appeal waiver, but I do not see the “clear, intentional relinquishment” necessary when the Government merely remains silent during a routine Rule 32(j)(1)(B) advisement and then promptly invokes the waiver on appeal. Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson are right to worry about defendant confusion from an unqualified “right to appeal” statement, yet under our cases the operative question is whether the defendant knowingly and voluntarily accepted the waiver at the Rule 11 colloquy; post-sentencing boilerplate cannot plausibly be treated as undoing that bargain or creating an administrable, reliance-based exception. Garza v. Idaho, as Justice Alito stresses, concerns counsel’s duty to file a notice of appeal despite a waiver, not a rule that generic advisements plus prosecutorial silence strip the Government of the benefit of its bargain. I would therefore affirm on narrow grounds—enforcing this waiver on these facts—without endorsing the Fifth Circuit’s broad suggestion that Rule 32(j) language and Government silence are categorically irrelevant in every case.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s forfeiture theory is the strongest counter, but it fails under ordinary waiver principles because forfeiture of a bargained-for appellate waiver requires a clear, intentional relinquishment, and the Government’s silence during a routine Rule 32(j)(1)(B) advisement is too equivocal to meet that standard—especially where, as the Chief Justice notes, the waiver was confirmed as knowing and voluntary at the Rule 11 colloquy and the Government promptly invoked the waiver on appeal. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance/fairness concerns do not supply a textual basis to treat the sentencing judge’s boilerplate “right to appeal” as expanding statutory appellate rights under § 3742 or altering the agreement’s terms; at most it is an imprecise notice of whatever residual rights remain. Garza v. Idaho, as Justice Alito emphasizes, concerns counsel’s duty to file a notice of appeal despite a waiver and does not convert generic post-sentencing language or prosecutorial silence into a nullification of an otherwise valid waiver. Under an originalist/textualist approach, absent clear text making Rule 32(j) advisements rights-conferring or waiver-nullifying, we should enforce the plea agreement as written and affirm.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s forfeiture framing is the most serious challenge, but it still cannot satisfy the required clarity for an intentional relinquishment: the Government’s silence during a routine Rule 32(j) advisement is too equivocal to surrender a bargained-for appellate waiver that the Government promptly invokes on appeal. As the Chief Justice notes, the sentencing judge’s unqualified “right to appeal” is best understood as boilerplate describing whatever residual rights remain, not as a moment that triggers forfeiture of the Government’s contractual benefit. Justice Sotomayor’s reasonable-reliance concern is real as a practical matter, but it does not negate the knowing-and-voluntary waiver confirmed at the Rule 11 colloquy, and I see no textual basis to create a contextual, case-by-case exception that would predictably erode administrable plea-waiver enforcement. Garza, as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, addresses counsel’s duty to file a notice of appeal despite a waiver, not a rule that generic post-sentencing advisements or prosecutorial inaction nullify enforcement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett fairly press that Rule 32(j) boilerplate should not be treated as rewriting a knowing-and-voluntary Rule 11 appeal waiver, and I agree Garza does not render waivers categorically unenforceable. But Justice Kagan’s narrower point remains dispositive for me: the Fifth Circuit’s categorical irrelevance rule improperly collapses ordinary waiver/forfeiture principles by treating an unqualified judicial “right to appeal” advisement—coupled with the Government’s silence at the critical moment—as incapable of mattering in any circumstance, even though it can predictably induce reliance by defendants deciding whether to file. The opposing side’s “intentional relinquishment” framing (Justice Alito/Justice Thomas) overstates what we need at this stage; the question is not contract modification but whether fairness and ordinary litigation principles require a contextual inquiry into forfeiture and reliance before using a waiver as a near-jurisdictional bar to reviewing liberty-restricting supervised-release conditions. On that basis, I would favor a remand for a contextual inquiry rather than automatic enforcement or automatic nullification.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett (and the Chief) are right that Rule 32(j) is a notice provision and does not itself modify a knowing-and-voluntary Rule 11 appeal waiver; I do not treat the judge’s boilerplate as “rewriting the bargain.” But that point does not answer the distinct question I raised: whether, under ordinary waiver/forfeiture principles, the Government’s conduct at the moment the court affirmatively triggers appellate decisionmaking can matter—and the Fifth Circuit’s categorical irrelevance rule improperly forecloses that inquiry. Justice Alito’s administrability concern is real, yet we can craft a narrow, workable standard focused on objectively clear indicia (unqualified judicial advisement plus prosecutorial acquiescence in context), without turning every sentencing script into litigation. Garza, as the Chief notes, does not invalidate waivers, but it reinforces that waivers do not erase the appellate process wholesale—supporting a remand for a contextual forfeiture/reliance assessment rather than automatic enforcement as if jurisdictional.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s forfeiture framing is the best argument for Petitioner, but it still lacks what ordinary waiver doctrine demands: a clear, intentional relinquishment of a known right. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett explain, Rule 32(j)(1)(B) is a generic notice provision and cannot be treated as a contract-modifying event; the Government’s silence amid boilerplate cannot reasonably be recast as an affirmative surrender of a bargained-for appellate waiver that was confirmed as knowing and voluntary at Rule 11. Garza, which Justices Sotomayor and Jackson invoke, is materially different—it requires counsel to file a notice of appeal despite a waiver, but it does not hold that post-sentencing misadvice or uncorrected advisements nullify an otherwise enforceable waiver when the Government promptly invokes it on appeal. Creating a contextual forfeiture-and-reliance inquiry here would invite litigation over sentencing-script phrasing rather than the waiver’s text and would weaken the administrable, text-centered rules plea bargaining depends upon.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that the Government can waive or forfeit reliance on an appeal waiver and that the Fifth Circuit should not speak in categorical terms about Rule 32(j) advisements being irrelevant in all circumstances. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett explain, forfeiture here requires a clear, intentional relinquishment, and the Government’s silence during a routine, court-delivered Rule 32(j)(1)(B) notice is too equivocal to amount to surrendering a bargained-for term that was confirmed as knowing and voluntary at the Rule 11 colloquy. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance/confusion concern is real, yet the better institutional and administrable rule is to read the generic “right to appeal” advisement as referring to whatever residual appellate rights remain under the waiver, rather than as triggering fact-intensive litigation over boilerplate sentencing scripts and prosecutor inaction. Garza, as Justice Alito notes, concerns counsel’s duty to file a notice of appeal despite a waiver and does not support treating post-sentencing boilerplate as nullifying an otherwise valid waiver that the Government promptly invokes on appeal.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s narrow forfeiture framing is the strongest counter: she is right that the Government can forfeit reliance on an appeal waiver, and that the Fifth Circuit should not speak as if a Rule 32(j) advisement is always irrelevant in every imaginable setting. But under ordinary waiver/forfeiture principles, forfeiture still requires conduct that fairly signals relinquishment, and the Government’s silence during a routine, court-delivered Rule 32(j)(1)(B) notice—after a Rule 11 colloquy confirmed a knowing-and-voluntary written waiver—does not clearly do that, especially when the Government promptly invokes the waiver on appeal (as the Chief Justice and Justice Alito stress). Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s reliance concerns underscore why district judges should be precise, yet the text and function of Rule 32(j) are notice-based and can naturally be read to describe only whatever residual appeal rights remain after the waiver, not to negate the waiver’s original public meaning or create an administrable, case-by-case exception. Garza, as Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh note, concerns counsel’s duty to file a notice of appeal notwithstanding a waiver and does not transform generic post-sentencing boilerplate into a Government forfeiture or a modification of the plea agreement.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s strongest point is administrability: a boilerplate Rule 32(j) advisement should not be treated as “rewriting the bargain,” and I agree it is not contract modification and does not automatically nullify a valid Rule 11 waiver. But Justice Kagan is right that the Fifth Circuit’s categorical irrelevance rule sweeps too broadly by foreclosing an ordinary waiver/forfeiture inquiry into the Government’s conduct at the critical moment the court affirmatively tells a defendant—without qualification—he has a “right to appeal,” and the waiver’s beneficiary says nothing. Respondents (Justice Barrett invoking Ricketts and Justice Alito emphasizing “intentional relinquishment”) persuasively protect plea bargains as binding exchanges, yet Ricketts does not address post-plea judicial misadvice plus prosecutorial acquiescence and the reliance/fairness concerns that go to whether enforcing the waiver as an absolute bar is consistent with procedural integrity. Garza does not make waivers unenforceable, but it undercuts treating them as jurisdictional-like extinguishers of the appellate process, supporting a narrow remand for a contextual inquiry rather than a categorical dismissal.

John Roberts.reasoning: A knowing-and-voluntary plea-agreement appeal waiver is generally enforceable as a matter of federal common-law contract principles and Rule 11 plea-colloquy protections, and nothing in Rule 32(j)(1)(B)’s post-sentencing advisement requirement suggests it can unilaterally rewrite the parties’ bargain. The sentencing judge’s generic statement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” without more, is best understood as a routine advisement that cannot override an earlier, valid waiver, particularly where the waiver’s text covers appeals “on any ground” other than ineffective assistance and thus encompasses a due-process challenge to supervised-release conditions. Enforcing the waiver here promotes institutional legitimacy and predictability in plea bargaining, consistent with our longstanding recognition that plea agreements are contractual in nature and should be enforced according to their terms. While the government can forfeit enforcement in particular cases, mere silence in response to a routine advisement is too thin a reed to find an intentional relinquishment of a bargained-for waiver, and a narrow ruling enforcing this waiver avoids creating a broad constitutional-claim carveout from waivers.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary appeal waiver in a plea agreement is enforceable according to its text, and nothing in 18 U.S.C. § 3742 or the Fifth Amendment affirmatively forbids waiver of appellate review of supervised-release conditions. Under ordinary plea-agreement enforcement principles, a district judge’s generic end-of-sentencing statement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” especially after a valid Rule 11 colloquy confirming the waiver, does not amend or nullify the parties’ bargain, and the government’s silence does not rewrite the agreement. Garza v. Idaho confirms that waivers are generally valid and enforceable while merely recognizing narrow limits (e.g., some claims may fall outside the waiver’s scope), and Ricketts v. Adamson underscores that plea bargains are binding exchanges that courts should enforce as written. Because petitioner’s due-process challenge falls within a broad waiver “on any ground” other than ineffective assistance, the court of appeals properly dismissed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of the plea agreement’s appeal waiver—knowingly and voluntarily accepted under Rule 11—controls, and it broadly bars an appeal challenging supervised-release conditions on due-process grounds absent an express exception. A district court’s generic end-of-sentencing advisement under Rule 32(j)(1)(B) that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” even if imprecise, does not unilaterally modify the parties’ bargain or nullify a previously valid waiver, particularly where the defendant still retains whatever limited appellate rights the waiver permits. Treating such boilerplate remarks as an implicit amendment would undermine the predictability and practical function of waivers in plea bargaining and impose substantial costs on the system, contrary to the contract-based enforcement principles recognized in Ricketts v. Adamson. Nothing in Garza v. Idaho suggests otherwise; Garza addresses counsel’s duty to file a notice of appeal despite a waiver, not the enforceability of the waiver itself on direct review.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A plea-agreement appeal waiver must be enforced only if it is knowing and voluntary under Rule 11 principles, and a sentencing court’s later, unqualified advisement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” coupled with the Government’s silence, reasonably creates confusion about what appellate rights remain and undermines strict enforcement of a boilerplate waiver as applied to a new due-process challenge to supervised-release conditions. Given the Due Process Clause interests implicated by supervised-release restrictions—often affecting liberty and reintegration—the Fifth Circuit’s near-categorical enforcement rule risks insulating constitutional error from any meaningful review, contrary to the judiciary’s duty to ensure fairness in sentencing under 18 U.S.C. § 3742’s framework for appellate review of sentences. Garza v. Idaho confirms that appeal waivers do not extinguish the appellate process wholesale and cautions against treating waivers as absolute in ways that deny practical access to review where the record indicates retained appellate rights or confusion. At minimum, where the district court affirmatively states an appeal right and the Government does not object, equity and the integrity of the plea process favor allowing appellate consideration of the due-process claim rather than dismissing on waiver grounds.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The plea waiver may be broad, but it remains a contractual and litigation right the government can waive or forfeit; a categorical rule that a judge’s post-sentencing advisement is “never relevant,” even when the government affirmatively acquiesces, is hard to square with ordinary waiver/forfeiture principles and Rule 11’s aim of ensuring knowing, voluntary, and workable plea practices. Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232 (2019), underscores that an appeal waiver does not extinguish appellate rights wholesale and cautions against mechanistic enforcement that ignores the real-world operation of appellate rights and actors’ duties; that logic supports at least a case-specific inquiry into whether the court’s “right to appeal” statement plus the government’s silence rendered enforcement inequitable or constituted a waiver of enforcement. Because the Fifth Circuit applied an absolute bar rather than a contextual analysis, I would vacate and remand to consider whether the government’s non-objection waived reliance on the appeal waiver and whether petitioner’s due-process challenge to a supervised-release condition may proceed under 18 U.S.C. § 3742. This approach respects the waiver’s text while preserving administrable, fair rules that do not force defendants to disregard the district court’s representations in open court.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plea agreement’s text controls: petitioner knowingly and voluntarily waived his right to appeal except for specified carveouts, and a due-process challenge to a supervised-release condition falls within that broad waiver as part of the sentence. Rule 11 confirms the waiver’s validity by requiring the court, before accepting the plea, to ensure the defendant understands any appeal-waiver provision, and Rule 11 does not permit a district court to unilaterally modify a plea agreement after acceptance (nor does Rule 32(j)’s generic notice create new appellate rights in derogation of the parties’ bargain). The sentencing judge’s later statement that petitioner “has a right to appeal,” even if imprecise, cannot rewrite the agreement, and the government’s silence is not mutual assent to modification under ordinary contract principles. Our cases treat plea agreements as bargained-for exchanges enforceable according to their terms, see Ricketts v. Adamson, and nothing in Garza v. Idaho suggests a valid waiver becomes unenforceable merely because a court later recites a general appellate-right advisement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: A knowing-and-voluntary appeal waiver in a plea agreement is generally enforceable as part of the bargain the parties struck, see Ricketts v. Adamson, 483 U.S. 1 (1987), and the waiver’s broad text here encompasses challenges to supervised-release conditions, including constitutional theories, absent an established exception. A district judge’s generic post-plea advisement at sentencing that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” without more, should not be treated as modifying the written plea agreement or nullifying an otherwise valid waiver under Rule 11 principles; at most it reflects that some limited appellate rights remain (e.g., ineffective-assistance claims). Although Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232 (2019), recognizes the government can forfeit reliance on a waiver, mere silence in response to a routine advisement is too slender a reed to deem the waiver waived—especially given institutional concerns for administrability and the settled practice of enforcing waivers to promote finality under 18 U.S.C. § 3742. Practical workability and respect for precedent counsel affirming enforcement of the waiver rather than creating a new, open-ended exception based on boilerplate sentencing remarks.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary plea-agreement appeal waiver is generally enforceable, and nothing in 18 U.S.C. § 3742 affirmatively indicates Congress barred such waivers; thus the waiver’s text controls and encompasses a due-process challenge to supervised-release conditions absent a specific carveout. Plea agreements are construed under contract principles and enforced according to their terms, see Ricketts v. Adamson, 483 U.S. 1, 8–10 (1987), and Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232, 238–239 (2019), recognizes both the validity of appeal waivers and that some appellate claims may remain only where the waiver does not cover them. A sentencing judge’s generic statement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” without more, does not modify the written agreement or render the prior waiver unknowing or involuntary under Rule 11 principles, particularly where the waiver was accepted during the plea colloquy. The government’s failure to object to that boilerplate advisement does not amount to a relinquishment of its contractual right to invoke the waiver on appeal.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Although plea-agreement appeal waivers are generally enforceable when entered knowingly and voluntarily, Garza v. Idaho recognizes that an appeal waiver does not extinguish all appellate rights and must be understood in context. Here, the sentencing court’s post-plea advisement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” coupled with the government’s failure to object, materially undermines the reliability of treating the waiver as an absolute bar at least to a due-process challenge to supervised-release conditions, where procedural fairness concerns are acute. Enforcing the waiver rigidly in these circumstances risks converting Rule 11’s emphasis on informed, voluntary relinquishment into a trap for the unwary and foreclosing review of constitutional error without clear notice at the decisive moment. I would therefore allow appellate review under 18 U.S.C. § 3742 notwithstanding the waiver, given the due-process framing and the reasonable reliance created by the court’s uncorrected instruction.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a criminal defendant’s broad appellate-rights waiver in a plea agreement remains enforceable when (a) he later appeals a supervised-release condition on due-process grounds and (b) the sentencing judge tells him he has a right to appeal without the government objecting.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1343 (wire fraud) and 18 U.S.C. § 2 (aiding and abetting) form the conviction background, but the dispute centers on enforceability of plea-agreement appeal waivers under federal plea-bargaining law (contract principles reflected in Fed. R. Crim. P. 11) and the Due Process Clause as invoked against an allegedly unlawful future supervised-release condition.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that the Fifth Circuit wrongly dismissed his appeal based on the plea’s appeal waiver because (1) the waiver should not be read to foreclose constitutional due-process challenges to supervised-release conditions—especially conditions that regulate future liberty and may be unlawful or insufficiently specified—and, in any event, (2) the district court’s unobjected-to statement at sentencing that petitioner “ha[d] a right to appeal” should be treated as negating or at least rendering ambiguous the waiver, so the waiver should not be enforced to bar appellate review.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues the waiver was knowing and voluntary and, by its terms, bars any appeal except ineffective-assistance claims; petitioner’s due-process challenge to a supervised-release condition falls within the waiver’s scope, and the judge’s routine end-of-sentencing remark about a right to appeal—especially absent any express modification of the plea agreement—does not nullify a valid waiver, so the Fifth Circuit correctly dismissed the appeal.

Ricketts v. Adamson, 483 U.S. 1 (1987)
Abney v. United States, 431 U.S. 651 (1977)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson raise the strongest point: due-process and Rule 11 concerns if a broad waiver, combined with an uncabined judicial statement that the defendant has a “right to appeal,” effectively insulates potentially unlawful supervised-release conditions from review. But as Justice Kagan explains, the better—and more administrable—reading of the Rule 32(j)-style advisement is that it refers to whatever appellate rights survive the waiver, and treating routine closing remarks (plus government silence) as creating waiver-undoing ambiguity would destabilize plea practice in a way Rule 11’s structure does not contemplate. Ricketts v. Adamson, emphasized by Justice Thomas and Justice Alito, reinforces that we generally enforce plea terms as written absent invalidity or breach, and Garza supports only the limited proposition that certain challenges (notably to the waiver’s validity) remain—rather than a categorical carveout for supervised-release conditions. A narrow holding enforcing this waiver on these facts, while preserving case-specific relief where the waiver is unknowing/ambiguous or the sentence exceeds statutory authority, best maintains institutional legitimacy without constitutionalizing a new exception.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s ambiguity point—that the judge’s unqualified Rule 32(j) advisement plus government silence could make the waiver unknowing—fails on the relevant text and structure: the plea agreement’s written waiver (with express carveouts) supplies the original public meaning of what was surrendered, and a judge’s routine advisement cannot alter that bargain without reopening Rule 11 and obtaining mutual assent. Justice Sotomayor’s due-process fairness concern about future liberty is serious, but it amounts to a request for a categorical constitutional exception for supervised-release conditions that neither the waiver’s text nor Garza v. Idaho supports; Garza preserves challenges to waiver validity, not an immunity for sentencing claims relabeled as due process. Consistent with Ricketts v. Adamson’s contract framework, enforcing a knowing and voluntary waiver as written promotes finality and respects the parties’ agreement absent breach or invalidity. Nothing in the record shows the waiver itself was involuntary, unknowing under Rule 11 at the time of the plea, or that the sentence exceeded statutory authority, so the appeal is barred.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s best point is that the judge’s uncabined statement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” coupled with government silence, could create confusion bearing on knowing-and-voluntary waiver, but I do not think that inference can overcome the written waiver and the Rule 11 colloquy that established assent to its broad terms. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, treating routine Rule 32(j)-style advisements as impliedly negating or amending a plea agreement would be unworkable and inconsistent with Rule 11’s limits on judicial alteration of plea terms; the court is not a party and did not reopen the bargain. Justice Sotomayor’s due-process fairness concern about insulating supervised-release conditions from review is serious, but under Garza (as Justice Kagan notes) the Constitution does not create a categorical carve-out for sentencing-condition challenges absent a defect in the waiver itself. Ricketts v. Adamson, emphasized by Justice Thomas, reinforces enforcing plea waivers as written to preserve finality and administrability while leaving defendants avenues to challenge waiver validity, statutory excess, breach, or ineffective assistance.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that Rule 32(j)’s generic advisement cannot, as a matter of contract modification, “rewrite” a plea waiver, and I do not rely on a unilateral-amendment theory. But Justice Jackson’s point underscores why the advisement still matters: it injects record ambiguity about what appellate review the defendant reasonably understood remained, and Rule 11’s knowing-and-voluntary requirement is a constitutional floor that contract analogies (including Justice Thomas’s reliance on Ricketts v. Adamson) do not displace. Garza v. Idaho reinforces that waivers are not categorical extinguishers of appellate rights, and given the future-liberty stakes of supervised-release conditions—often not fully foreseeable at the plea stage—due process counsels against enforcing this waiver to insulate potentially unlawful conditions from any meaningful review. On my pragmatic approach, finality interests cannot justify enforcing a waiver where the court’s own unqualified assurance, coupled with the government’s silence, makes it unclear that this specific forfeiture was understood and voluntary.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that the district court’s uncaveated “right to appeal,” plus government silence, could create real-world confusion bearing on whether the waiver was knowing and voluntary—but on this record that concern is better handled through the existing validity/ambiguity inquiry rather than treating routine Rule 32(j) advisements as undoing a written waiver. Justice Sotomayor’s due-process argument about insulating unconstitutional supervised-release conditions is serious, yet Garza v. Idaho (as the Chief Justice emphasizes) preserves challenges to the waiver’s validity and counsel’s obligations without constitutionalizing a categorical carveout for sentencing-condition claims. And as Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett note, reading generic advisements as implied amendment would destabilize Rule 11 practice by making enforceability turn on boilerplate sentencings rather than the plea text and colloquy. Under a pragmatic textualist approach, the most coherent, workable rule is to enforce clear waivers while leaving open traditional avenues (invalid waiver, breach, ineffective assistance, or statutory-excess sentences) for genuinely unlawful conditions.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that the court’s unqualified Rule 32(j) advisement, coupled with government silence, could create confusion bearing on whether the waiver was knowing and voluntary. But under Rule 11’s text and our plea-agreement precedents, the relevant inquiry is whether the waiver was knowing and voluntary at the time it was entered and accepted—not whether later, routine sentencing boilerplate introduced ambiguity; otherwise (as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress) standard advisements would unpredictably destabilize bargained-for waivers. Justice Sotomayor’s due-process concern about supervised-release conditions affecting future liberty is substantial, but creating a categorical constitutional carveout would, as Justice Thomas notes via Ricketts v. Adamson, depart from enforcing the agreement’s terms absent invalidity or breach, and Garza v. Idaho does not constitutionalize new exceptions beyond challenges to the waiver’s validity. On this record, the waiver’s broad language still covers the sentencing-condition appeal, and the court’s post-plea statement cannot rewrite the parties’ bargain.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s point that the district judge’s uncaveated “right to appeal” statement (and the Government’s silence) could create Rule 11 ambiguity is the strongest pushback, but I read that advisement—consistent with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan—as a generic Rule 32(j)-style notice referring to whatever limited rights survive a broad waiver, not as evidence the waiver was unknowing or involuntary. Justice Sotomayor’s due-process concern about insulating future-liberty supervised-release conditions from review is serious, yet Garza v. Idaho (as Justice Kagan emphasizes) preserves challenges to the waiver’s validity and other established exceptions; it does not justify crafting a categorical constitutional carveout that would destabilize settled plea-bargaining practice. Ricketts v. Adamson, highlighted by Justice Thomas, reinforces the Court’s consistent contract-like enforcement of plea terms absent breach or invalidity, and Rule 11 does not authorize unilateral post-acceptance modification by the court. On this record, enforcing the waiver as written best accords with precedent, administrability, and institutional legitimacy while leaving defendants avenues to challenge invalid waivers or unlawful sentences outside the waiver’s scope.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s ambiguity point—that the judge’s unqualified Rule 32(j) advisement plus government silence could undermine the waiver’s knowing-and-voluntary character—is the strongest pushback, but on a textualist view the operative relinquishment is the written waiver accepted under Rule 11, and routine sentencing advisements are best read (as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice explain) to mean whatever limited appellate rights survive. Treating such advisements as generating “reasonable confusion” sufficient to nullify an otherwise clear waiver would effectively create an administrability-problematic, judge-dependent exception untethered to the plea’s text and Rule 11’s controlled colloquy. Justice Sotomayor’s due-process concern about insulating unconstitutional supervised-release conditions is serious, yet Garza—as Justice Roberts notes—supports enforcing waivers according to their terms while preserving established avenues (invalid waiver, breach, ineffective assistance), not crafting a categorical carveout for constitutional sentencing-condition claims. Ricketts v. Adamson, emphasized by Justice Thomas and Justice Alito, reinforces that we do not revise plea bargains after the fact absent a defect in assent, and nothing in this record shows the waiver itself was defective.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s point that Rule 11 does not permit a district judge to unilaterally rewrite a plea agreement, and I agree with Justice Kagan that treating every routine Rule 32(j) appeal advisement as a contractual amendment would be unworkable. But my view does not depend on “modification”; it turns on Rule 11’s knowing-and-voluntary requirement and the practical fairness consequences when the court affirmatively tells the defendant—without tying it to the waiver—that he “has a right to appeal,” and the Government (which did bargain for the waiver) remains silent, leaving an ambiguity in the record about what rights were actually understood to be surrendered. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Ricketts v. Adamson and contract-like enforcement principles is relevant, yet plea waivers operate in a constitutional procedure, and under Garza v. Idaho waivers are not all-purpose extinguishers; enforcing this waiver despite court-created confusion risks insulating potentially unlawful supervised-release restraints on future liberty from any meaningful review. On this record, I would resolve that ambiguity against forfeiture and allow the appeal to proceed.

John Roberts.reasoning: A knowing-and-voluntary appeal waiver in a plea agreement is generally enforceable according to its terms, and Rule 11 does not authorize a district court to unilaterally revise that bargain after acceptance; absent mutual assent to modification, the waiver remains binding under ordinary contract principles reflected in federal plea practice. The sentencing court’s generic advisement that the defendant “has a right to appeal” can be understood as referring to whatever limited appellate rights remain notwithstanding the waiver, and the government’s failure to object does not itself alter the written agreement. Enforcing the waiver here also serves institutional legitimacy by honoring negotiated pleas and avoiding broad constitutional carve-outs for supervised-release conditions that are foreseeable and can be addressed through narrow exceptions already recognized in waiver doctrine. This approach is consistent with the Court’s emphasis that plea agreements are to be enforced as written and that defendants may waive appellate rights as part of the bargain.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: A plea agreement is a bargained-for instrument whose written terms control, and a knowing and voluntary appellate-rights waiver is enforceable according to its text unless the agreement itself is breached or invalid. Under Ricketts v. Adamson, 483 U.S. 1 (1987), courts generally apply contract principles to plea agreements, so a sentencing judge’s routine advisement that the defendant has a “right to appeal”—absent any textual modification of the plea agreement—does not negate an express waiver, nor does the Government’s silence rewrite the contract. The Due Process Clause does not supply a free-floating exception to a broad waiver that, by its terms, forecloses “any appeal” except ineffective-assistance claims; enforcing the waiver respects the defendant’s bargain and the limited judicial role under Fed. R. Crim. P. 11. Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232 (2019), confirms that waivers do not extinguish all rights in all contexts, but it does not authorize disregarding an otherwise valid waiver to reach the merits of a waived sentencing challenge.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The plea agreement’s appellate-rights waiver should be enforced according to its text where it was knowing and voluntary and broadly forecloses appeals except for specified claims; nothing in Fed. R. Crim. P. 11 authorizes a district court to unilaterally revise an accepted plea agreement at sentencing. A routine post-sentencing advisement that the defendant has a right to appeal—especially without any mutual assent by the parties—does not modify the bargain or estop the government from invoking the waiver, because the court is not a party to the contract and Rule 11 “strictly limits the role of the court” in plea bargaining. Nor does styling the challenge as “due process” remove it from the waiver’s scope; defendants may prospectively waive constitutional and statutory appellate claims in exchange for the benefits of the plea, consistent with the contract principles recognized in Ricketts v. Adamson. Enforcing the waiver promotes the practical consequences Congress and Rule 11 contemplate—finality and efficient administration of justice—without expanding appellate review beyond what the defendant expressly surrendered.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A general appeal waiver cannot be treated as an absolute bar to appellate review of constitutional defects in sentencing, particularly supervised-release conditions that will govern future liberty and may be unlawfully vague or imposed without adequate notice; Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232, 238 (2019), confirms that waivers do not categorically extinguish appellate rights. Given the Due Process Clause interests implicated by supervised-release conditions, enforcing the waiver here would risk insulating potentially unlawful restraints on liberty from any meaningful review, contrary to basic fairness and the judiciary’s responsibility to prevent unjust sentences. Moreover, the district court’s on-the-record advisement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” coupled with the government’s silence, at minimum creates ambiguity about whether the waiver would be enforced in this circumstance, and Rule 11’s insistence on a knowing, voluntary waiver counsels against strict enforcement where the court’s own statements reasonably suggest otherwise. The practical, real-world impact of denying review is to leave vulnerable defendants subject to potentially unconstitutional conditions without a remedy, a cost too high to pay for finality.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under ordinary plea-agreement principles reflected in Fed. R. Crim. P. 11, a knowing and voluntary appellate-rights waiver is enforceable according to its terms, and petitioner’s due-process challenge to a supervised-release condition is a challenge to the sentence that falls within a broad waiver’s scope absent an explicit carveout. Garza v. Idaho emphasizes that appeal waivers are not “absolute” and that some claims (including challenges to the waiver’s own validity) remain available, but it expressly declines to constitutionalize any particular set of exceptions beyond that baseline; this case presents no showing that the waiver itself was unknowing or involuntary. The sentencing judge’s generic statement that petitioner had a right to appeal, without any express modification of the plea agreement and without a Rule 11 colloquy re-opening the waiver, does not plausibly rewrite the bargain; treating such routine remarks as nullifying waivers would be unworkable and inconsistent with enforcing negotiated agreements. The Fifth Circuit therefore could dismiss the appeal pursuant to the waiver, while leaving petitioner the ability to contest the waiver’s validity or raise claims (like ineffective assistance) that the agreement preserved.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: A plea agreement is a contract-like instrument enforced according to its terms when entered knowingly and voluntarily, and nothing in Rule 11 or the Due Process Clause authorizes courts to rewrite a broad waiver to create a freestanding constitutional exception for supervised-release conditions. Garza v. Idaho recognizes that appeal waivers are not absolute, but it expressly declined to specify what exceptions are required, and it does not suggest that a routine end-of-sentencing advisement can nullify a written waiver absent an actual modification of the plea’s terms. The district judge’s generic statement that the defendant has a “right to appeal,” without more, cannot override the parties’ bargain or alter the separation-of-powers allocation that leaves charging and plea concessions to the Executive and adjudication to the Judiciary. Enforcing the waiver as written respects the plain meaning of the agreement and the settled understanding (reflected in Ricketts v. Adamson) that defendants and the Government are entitled to the benefit of their bargain.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary appeal waiver in a Rule 11 plea agreement is generally enforceable under ordinary contract-like principles, and nothing in the Due Process Clause creates a categorical exemption for supervised-release-condition challenges when the waiver’s text broadly covers “any appeal” (with narrow carveouts such as ineffective assistance). Ricketts v. Adamson confirms the Court’s longstanding practice of holding defendants and the Government to the bargains they struck, and Garza v. Idaho—while recognizing that some appellate rights persist despite waivers—does not suggest that courts should treat routine Rule 32(j) end-of-sentencing advisements as impliedly rewriting a plea agreement. A sentencing judge’s generic statement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” without an express modification and without the Government’s assent, should not nullify the waiver because that would undermine workability and predictability in plea bargaining and invite post hoc uncertainty. The defendant may still pursue any claims outside the waiver’s scope (e.g., ineffective assistance) and can raise objections to supervised-release conditions at sentencing, preserving judicial restraint and institutional stability while respecting the parties’ agreement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary appellate-rights waiver is generally enforceable according to its terms, and nothing in Fed. R. Crim. P. 11 authorizes a district court to unilaterally modify a plea agreement after acceptance through a generic post-sentencing advisement about a “right to appeal.” Under ordinary contract principles applied to plea bargains, modification requires mutual assent; a routine statement at sentencing—especially one consistent with the existence of whatever limited appellate rights remain—does not negate an otherwise clear waiver, and the government’s silence does not supply assent. Petitioner’s due-process challenge to a supervised-release condition is still an appeal from the sentence and thus falls within a broad waiver unless the waiver’s text preserves constitutional claims (which this one does not). Ricketts v. Adamson underscores that plea agreements are enforced according to their terms absent a basis to set them aside, and nothing here overcomes the waiver’s plain scope.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Although appeal waivers in plea agreements are generally enforceable when knowing and voluntary, this Court has emphasized that such waivers do not extinguish all appellate entitlements and must be applied with attention to fairness and what was actually surrendered. See Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232, 238-239 (2019). Here, the defendant’s due-process challenge targets a supervised-release condition governing future liberty, and the sentencing judge’s unobjected-to statement that he “ha[d] a right to appeal” reasonably creates at least ambiguity as to whether appellate review of that condition remained available under Rule 11’s fairness-and-clarity framework for plea proceedings. Given the practical consequences of insulating potentially unlawful liberty-restricting conditions from review and the government’s silence in the face of the court’s advisement, I would not enforce the waiver to bar this due-process appeal.
